quote: The nations have come, O God
note: Psalm 79 (78 in the Latin Bible), given in Latin in Dante's text: "Deus, venerunt gentes". It mourns the Temple of Jerusalem, defiled and ruined by foreign armies. The virtues sing it over the Church, which has just been carried off.
The three theological virtues and the four cardinal virtues take turns, verse by verse, as two halves of a choir chant a psalm.

context: Beatrice's grief over the Church is set beside Mary's as she stood at the foot of the cross and watched her son die.

note: The flush of righteous anger. Grief gives way to the certainty that the wrong will be punished.

quote: A little while, and you will not see me
note: Christ's words to his disciples at the Last Supper, foretelling his death and resurrection (John 16:16). Beatrice speaks them in Latin. The true Church will be lost to sight for a time, and then return.
The lady of the garden, who will at last be given a name later in this canto.

context: The one poet still at Dante's side now that Virgil is gone.

note: Her first tender word to him. The trial is over, and she speaks now as a teacher, and as one saved soul to another.
The chariot, whose floor the dragon tore out in Canto 32: the Church.
The words Revelation uses of the beast: "the beast that you saw was, and is not" (17:8). Beatrice turns them on the Church. As the thing Christ founded, it no longer exists.

Dante's Italian says God's vengeance "fears no sops". Early commentators explain it by a custom: a murderer who managed to eat a sop of bread and wine on his victim's grave within nine days was thought safe from the family's revenge. No such trick will work against God.
The Roman Empire, whose gifts of wealth and power turned the Church first into a monster and then into the prey of the French king.

Dante held that the imperial throne had been empty in all but name since Frederick II died in 1250, because the emperors after him never came to Italy to rule. His hopes for an heir settled on Henry VII, who entered Italy in 1310 and died there in 1313.

quote: a Five Hundred, Ten, and Five
note: The poem's most famous riddle. In Roman numerals the number is DXV, and the letters rearranged spell DVX, Latin for "leader". It answers the 666 of the beast in Revelation. Who the leader is has never been settled: the emperor Henry VII, Cangrande della Scala of Verona, or Christ at his return are the usual guesses. Like the Greyhound of Inferno 1, he is a deliverer still to come.
The whore of Canto 32, the corrupt papacy, which has taken a place that is not hers. The giant is the French crown.

Dante names two riddlers here, Themis and the Sphinx. Themis was a goddess whose oracle spoke in dark sayings. The Sphinx was the monster of Thebes that killed everyone who could not answer its riddle, until Oedipus did.

In Ovid's Metamorphoses, after the Sphinx's riddle was solved, a beast was sent to ravage the herds and fields of Thebes. This riddle will be solved at no such cost. Dante says the events will be its "Naiads": his copy of Ovid had a scribe's error that made the water nymphs, not Oedipus, the solvers.
One of the poem's best-known definitions of earthly life. The thought is an old Christian one: Saint Augustine wrote that our whole life is nothing but a race toward death.
First by Adam, who took its fruit. The second time is in the scenes just shown, when the eagle tore through its branches and the chariot that had been bound to it was dragged away.

context: In Paradiso 26 Adam gives the count himself: 930 years of life on earth and 4,302 in Limbo, until Christ came down to free him.

quote: Him who punished the bite in Himself
note: Christ, who took the penalty for Adam's sin on himself by dying on the cross.

The tree widens as it rises, so that it cannot be climbed. Its height and its shape both say: do not touch. In the moral sense, Beatrice says, the tree is God's justice, shown in the command he gave and the obedience he asked.
Dante names the Elsa, a river in Tuscany whose water is so full of lime that things left in it are coated with a crust of stone. Worldly thoughts have done the same to his mind.

The Italian has a second comparison from Ovid: the pleasure Dante took in those thoughts stained his mind as the blood of Pyramus stained the white mulberry dark. Pyramus killed himself under a mulberry tree, believing his beloved Thisbe dead (Purgatorio 27).

Pilgrims back from the Holy Land carried a staff bound with palm leaves, as proof of where they had been. Dante is to carry her words home in the same way, even if he keeps only their outline and not yet their meaning.
Usually read as philosophy, the human learning Dante gave himself to in the years after Beatrice died. It is not condemned, but it cannot reach what she is teaching now, which comes from revelation.

In the Italian, the heaven "that spins fastest": the Primum Mobile, the outermost of the turning spheres. The comparison echoes Isaiah 55:9: "As the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways."

context: Beatrice's proof, made with a smile. Lethe takes away only the memory of sin. If Dante has forgotten that he ever left her, then leaving her was a sin.

note: A promise kept in Paradiso, where Beatrice explains instead of prophesying. The riddles end with this canto.

It is noon, when the sun is highest, seems brightest and appears to move most slowly. The meridian is the line it crosses at midday, and it differs for every place on earth. This is the Wednesday after Easter, 1300, the journey's seventh day.
Two of the four rivers that flow out of Eden in Genesis 2. The two streams Dante sees are Lethe and Eunoe, rising from one spring and parting.

quote: O light, O glory of humankind
note: Dante's address to Beatrice.

context: Named here for the first and only time, five cantos after Dante met her. The Italian form of the name is Matelda.

quote: This and other things I told him
note: In Canto 28 she explained both rivers to Dante, and what each one does.

context: The last act of the climb. Lethe has taken the memory of Dante's sins, and Eunoe now gives back, at full strength, the memory of the good he has done.

note: Statius drinks too. This is the last the poem says of him. His climb is finished, and he goes on to Heaven.
One of some twenty places where Dante turns to speak to his reader directly.

The poem is built to a plan: one opening canto, then thirty-three each for Hell, Purgatory and Heaven, a hundred in all. This is the thirty-third of Purgatorio, and Dante lets the design itself cut him short.
The Italian says "new" three times in two lines: new plants, renewed with new leaves. The tree in Canto 32 flowered again in the same way.
Inferno, Purgatorio and Paradiso all end on the same word, "stelle", stars. At the end of Inferno Dante came out to see them again. Now he is ready to rise among them.
